extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency officials, policymakers, and practitioners interested in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and procedural standards for how agencies should treat, process, and respond to public comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking, with particular attention to mass/form comments and value-laden (policy) comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency obligation to respond to significant issues raised in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are responsible for responding to significant issues raised in comments, including those comments identifying a technical difficulty with a rule or transmitting scientific information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts reviewing under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard focus on the rational connection between facts found and agency choices; an agency’s failure to acknowledge substantive technical or factual issues may lead to vacatur (see Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm; United States v. Nova Scotia Food Prods. Corp.; Portland Cement Ass’n v. Ruckelshaus). By contrast, purely speculative comments that do not disclose a factual or policy basis require no response. Agencies therefore must identify and respond to "significant" technical or factual objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full public notice and the 'logical outgrowth' constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must give full public notice of all critical matters contemplated for a final rule; any rule change in response to comments that is beyond a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposed rule either makes the rule vulnerable to judicial invalidation or requires a new round of notice and comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This APA §553(b)-driven constraint creates incentives for agencies to resolve critical issues prior to issuing the notice of proposed rulemaking; as a result, agencies often treat proposals as 'set' at the proposed-rule stage, paying more attention to technical adjustments than to value-focused changes that would be a nonlogical outgrowth (see Fertilizer Inst. v. EPA). The constraint explains why only technical comments that suggest permissible modifications are likely to be adopted without further notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial incentives favor engagement with technical/scientific comments over value-focused comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review requirements give agencies an incentive to take technical comments more seriously than value-focused comments because courts look for factual and scientific bases tying agency choices to agency findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, agencies tend to respond exhaustively to technical or evidentiary objections but give less weight or less detailed reply to value-laden, preference-based comments. Research has not uncovered successful challenges vacating agency action solely for failing to consider mass expressions of public preference; courts have made clear agencies are not required to follow the weight of commenter preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for when multiple value-laden comments deserve especial attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies might consider the following criteria for deciding when multiple value-laden comments deserve especial attention: (1) comments submitted are particularly numerous, (2) a particular viewpoint represents a strong majority or a supermajority of the comments filed, (3) the comments raise an issue relevant under the agency’s statutory authorization, (4) the comments are coherent and persuasive, and (5) the comments point in a different direction from that considered by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many comments point in a direction different from the agency’s proposed path, they can be an important signal—perhaps akin to a straw poll—indicating that further investigation into public values and policy direction is needed. These criteria are proposed as a systematic way to decide when mass value-focused input merits heightened engagement, without turning comment counts into a referendum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prenotice participation cannot substitute for notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Prenotice participation (consultation before publication of the proposed rule) is not an adequate substitute for the statutorily mandated notice-and-comment process; parties who participate prenotice often include a disproportionate number of regulated entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies frequently consult regulated entities prenotice—who provide useful technical information and with whom agencies have existing contacts—members of the public who did not participate prenotice may find their later comments get less attention, especially if adopting them would require significant revision. Agencies should not let prenotice engagement become a way to exclude lay or diffuse beneficiary input from substantive consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing and treating form/identical (high-volume) comments and astroturfing risk
rubrics_metrics.description: High volumes of form letters or identical emails raise questions about duplication, authenticity, and possible 'astroturfing'; agencies often observe many duplications and may not keep exact counts of duplicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identical or near-identical text may undermine the impression that each submission conveys a deeply held individual view, but it still conveys more information than a simple vote or a 'Like'. Agencies may take steps to reduce manipulation risk—e.g., require affirmations that commenters are not paid, limit anonymous comments, encourage individualization of submissions, or use tools to identify nonidentical content. Outsourcing or automated deduplication may be employed to manage volume, but agencies must be wary of giving high-volume comments short shrift simply because they are numerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology and resource management in processing mass comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies facing thousands or millions of comments may outsource or automate reading and analysis, and may use analytic tools to distill comment content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the Rule-Writer’s Workbench and other analytical software used to analyze comments (e.g., Fish and Wildlife Service for polar bear listing). While technology can help identify unique substantive input, resource constraints and reliance on automation create temptations to short-change high-volume comment sets; agencies should design processes that surface substantive content rather than merely trimming volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to statutory authorization as a threshold for consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments deserve consideration insofar as they raise issues relevant under the agency’s statutory authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a large volume of comments that fall outside the scope of what the agency is authorized to consider should not be given dispositive weight; relevance to the enabling statute is a key filter for whether value-laden or other comments can legitimately influence rule content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical weight of commenters is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency is not obligated to take the approach advocated by the largest number of commenters; rulemaking is not a process in which 'the majority of commenters prevail by sheer weight of numbers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have upheld that agencies are free to adopt policies contrary to the majority of commenters. Relying solely on comment counts as a referendum invites manipulation (astroturfing) and would distort the deliberative function of rulemaking; agencies should instead assess content, relevance, coherence, and statutory fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative comments lacking factual or policy basis need not be answered
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments which are purely speculative and do not disclose the factual or policy basis on which they rest require no response from the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle—supported by case law—means agencies can focus finite response resources on comments that present factual, technical, or legally significant challenges rather than on speculative or unsupported assertions. However, agencies should still be careful not to label substantively meaningful value-claims as merely 'speculative.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to engage value-focused comments undermines legitimacy and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic disregard for value-laden public comments, especially mass comments, can undermine the democratic legitimacy of agency decisions and reduce public willingness to accept outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because public comments convey crystallized, concrete preferences (more so than votes), ignoring them can discourage participation and encourage agencies to hide policy choices within technical analyses. Engaging these comments—when relevant and coherent—can improve transparency and the perceived responsiveness of agencies, even if agencies are not required to adopt the majority’s preferred outcome.
